newsitem.title: CANADA: Bre-X listed in Toronto with little disclosure.
newsitem.headline: Bre-X listed in Toronto with little disclosure.

text.p: Bre-X Minerals Ltd. was listed last year on the Toronto Stock Exchange -- Canada's biggest -- although it had not issued a prospectus since 1989 when it started as a penny stock on the Alberta Exchange.

The TSE's apparent willingness to list companies despite such minimal disclosure is being questioned after the admission by Calgary, Alberta-based Bre-X that it may have overstated the size of its gold discovery on the Indonesian island of Borneo.

The TSE insists it has the most stringent listing requirements in Canada. But Bre-X's only prospectus was issued in May 1989 when it went public, selling one million shares at C30 cents (22 cents) each on the Alberta Exchange, Canada's smallest.

Critics said that the TSE would accept virtually any company with a listing on another exchange, particularly small or speculative mining and exploration concerns that attracted high trading volumes and thus boosted profit for the exchange.

"They've got this bogus entrance requirement and it's allowing companies to interlist on Toronto, even though they are basically looking for something big and spectacular that will lead to a buyout by a major mining company," said John Kaiser, the editor of a California-based newsletter.
He said the TSE benefited from a misperception among investors that it required more substantial disclosure than smaller exchanges.

"Institutions seem to think that a TSE listing makes that TSE stock a better or safer investment than a Vancouver stock. And I don't think there is any basis for this sort of assumption," Kaiser said.

The Bre-X debacle is a spectacular case in point. The company has said that its Busang property in Indonesia contained at least 71 million ounces of gold -- valued at around $20 billion at current bullion prices.

Almost C$3 billion ($2.19 billion) was lopped off Bre-X's market value in a few minutes of frenzied selling last week after reports from the prospector's new partner that Busang appeared to contain very little gold.

The TSE said it required mining firms to have proven reserves for a mine life of at least three years. They must have a program of exploration or development on a property where "results indicate at least continuity of mineralization in three dimensions at economically interesting grades."
The TSE's capital requirements for a listing are also higher than those of other Canadian exchanges. But Kaiser said that companies could simply list on a small exchange to help fund a TSE listing.

"Lately what we've been seeing is a migration of companies from the smaller exchanges onto the TSE. They've been heavily bankrolled at the CDN (Canadian Dealing Network) or the ASE (Alberta Stock Exchange), VSE (Vancouver Stock Exchange) level, and they've managed to acquire some sort of deposit which they can talk about economic potential," Kaiser said.
Bre-X, which has never produced any gold, but attracted huge sums from investors, was among 168 companies to list on the TSE last year.
TSE President Rowland Fleming said on Tuesday the exchange was examining the Bre-X debacle closely, but he declined to say if it might strengthen its listing requirements.
But he added that "it would be naive of you to believe that the extraordinary circumstances here have not heightened the state of alert in our market surveillance department."
Some market players believed the TSE's listing requirements were strict enough and that it had enough experience in the mining sector to safeguard investors.

"(The listing requirements) seem fairly stringent to me. Who knows the mining business and mining financing business better than Canadians?" said Fred Ketchen, director of equity trading at ScotiaMcLeod Inc. and past chairman of the TSE.
"Stock exchanges can't run these companies and they can't have a person on sight checking everything that comes through," Ketchen said.

"It may well be that somewhere down the way there are going to be changes made by the regulators in how they treat this kind of stuff. Nevertheless in the meantime you've got to rely on the integrity of the people involved with these companies."
